topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - nature.com
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; findings on digital competencies may have limited direct application to other sectors or non-European settings, though competency frameworks often have transferable principles.
takeaways: Review competency frameworks specifically designed for digital health roles in your sector to identify which technical and soft skills are most valued in Europe — this can inform capability-building priorities.

Consider whether the European digital public health competencies identified are relevant to your organisation's AI literacy program, or whether sector-specific adaptations are needed for your workforce.
Use the scoping review's competency taxonomy to benchmark current employee capabilities against evidence-based standards, helping prioritize upskilling gaps.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - nature.com
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; generalisability to adult workplace AI literacy development or other educational levels unclear. Geographic scope not specified from available information.
takeaways: AI literacy in education should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, helping learners understand AI's role alongside other digital competencies.

Develop age-appropriate AI competency standards for middle school that bridge foundational digital skills and practical AI understanding, which could inform scaffolding approaches for adult learners new to AI.
Consider how educators' own AI literacy gaps may constrain curriculum delivery — professional development pathways for teachers are as critical as student frameworks.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on public health faculty development; generalisability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear. The approach may be specific to higher education contexts.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption in public health can be reframed as a development opportunity — structured professional development programs that address knowledge gaps and concerns are more effective than top-down mandates.

Invest in targeted faculty training that moves educators from skepticism to capability; this is foundational before expecting them to teach AI literacy to students or implement AI tools in their curriculum.

Design change management processes that acknowledge educator concerns, build competence incrementally, and create peer learning communities to sustain readiness for AI integration in public health education.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect clients of a large consulting firm and may skew toward larger, well-resourced organisations.
takeaways: AI adoption requires deliberate workforce capability building, not just technology deployment — map current skills gaps and design targeted upskilling pathways aligned to your organisation's AI strategy.

Workforce transformation must address both technical literacy (understanding AI tools and limitations) and adaptive capability (comfort with change, collaboration with AI systems) — prioritise psychological safety and role clarity to ease transitions.

Early identification of high-risk roles and affected teams allows you to plan reskilling, redeployment, or transition support proactively rather than reactively, reducing disruption and retaining institutional knowledge.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on higher education context; applicability to corporate or organisational settings outside academia would require adaptation.
takeaways: AI literacy functions as a meta-skill that integrates multiple domains rather than a single technical competency — consider developing multi-domain training programmes that address conceptual understanding, technical foundations, critical thinking, and organisational application together.

The four-domain model provides a structured framework for designing AI capability development in academic management roles — use this taxonomy to audit gaps in your current AI upskilling programmes and identify which domains are underrepresented.

Positioning AI literacy as foundational for academic innovation suggests that general staff, not just technical roles, need access to AI literacy development — evaluate whether your organisation's AI training is inclusive or siloed to specific departments.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education sector, which may not directly translate to corporate workplace learning contexts. Geographic scope unclear from title alone.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your organisation's roles and design targeted development pathways rather than generic AI literacy programmes.

Consider adopting higher education's pedagogical approaches (e.g. project-based learning, cross-disciplinary collaboration) to make AI competency development more engaging and practical for employees.
Assess current skill gaps across your workforce to prioritise which competencies to develop first, rather than attempting comprehensive AI upskilling simultaneously.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — would depend on sample composition, industry sectors studied, and geographic scope, which cannot be determined from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may have mixed effects on employee creativity — understanding both positive and negative mechanisms is essential before implementation to mitigate unintended downsides.

Assess how your organisation's AI tools might constrain creative thinking (e.g., through over-reliance on automation or narrowed problem-solving approaches) and design complementary practices to preserve and stimulate innovation.
When rolling out AI capabilities, monitor employee creativity metrics alongside productivity gains to identify whether the technology is enhancing or inhibiting the creative contribution you value.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - nature.com
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professions or sectors without further research. The three-wave design strengthens causal inference, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear from the snippet.
takeaways: Design AI implementation initiatives in healthcare settings to preserve or enhance clinician autonomy — the data suggest that readiness alone does not improve wellbeing unless staff retain meaningful control over how they work with AI tools.

When rolling out medical AI, prioritise transparent communication about how AI will affect decision-making authority and task ownership for nurses; loss of autonomy appears to be the mechanism linking AI readiness to wellbeing outcomes.

Monitor nurse wellbeing longitudinally during AI transitions; this study demonstrates that the relationship between readiness and wellbeing unfolds over time and is mediated by perceived autonomy rather than being immediate or direct.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and sector representation, which are not indicated in the snippet. The theoretical framework around role ambiguity and self-efficacy in AI collaboration is likely applicable across knowledge-work sectors, but geographic scope and specific industry context are unclear.
takeaways: Role ambiguity—uncertainty about how AI should be used and what employees are responsible for—appears to be a key barrier to effective employee-AI collaboration; clarifying expectations and use cases upfront can reduce this friction.

Self-efficacy (confidence in one's ability to work with AI) is a distinct and likely modifiable factor; targeted training and low-risk practice opportunities may strengthen it independently of role clarity.
These are dual, potentially independent pathways affecting AI adoption; addressing only one (e.g., building skills without clarifying roles) may not solve adoption or collaboration problems.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox may apply broadly to knowledge work, but without seeing the full study design, sample characteristics, and geographic scope, applicability across different sectors and regions cannot be assessed.
takeaways: Generative AI can create competing effects on how employees share and use knowledge — some roles may see automation reduce knowledge-sharing behaviours while others experience augmentation that enhances collaborative learning. Diagnose which effect is occurring in your teams before designing interventions.

The 'paradox' suggests that simply deploying AI tools without addressing underlying knowledge-sharing incentives or role clarity may inadvertently discourage employees from contributing expertise. Pair AI adoption with explicit expectations about knowledge contribution and psychological safety around AI use.

articles.title: How rejection letters from AI recruiters shape recruiter's prestige and experienced respect - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How rejection letters from AI recruiters shape recruiter's prestige and experienced respect  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident. Generalisability depends on whether study involved real AI recruitment systems, job seekers across sectors, and whether findings apply beyond the specific AI tool tested.
takeaways: AI-generated rejection communications may inadvertently affect how candidates perceive recruiter credibility and professionalism; consider how your organisation's AI rejection messaging is framed to maintain trust and respect.

Rejection letters from AI systems carry psychological weight similar to human-delivered rejections; ensure tone, clarity, and empathy in automated communications to minimise candidate frustration and protect employer brand.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects American workplace context and APA perspectives. Findings and recommendations may not directly transfer to Australian employment law, industrial relations frameworks, or workplace culture.
takeaways: Acknowledge that AI-driven workplace change creates genuine psychological uncertainty for employees; leaders should proactively communicate about role transitions and job security to reduce anxiety and maintain psychological safety.
Use this as a prompt to assess your organisation's change management approach — do you have clear communication channels, reskilling pathways, and mental health support in place as AI is implemented?

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner report likely drawing on client work across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific methodologies and sample characteristics are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (technology-first) to 'AI adaptation' (behaviour-first) to better engage employees in the change process and build required capabilities.

Identify and design interventions targeting the specific human behaviours and mindsets needed for effective AI use, rather than assuming adoption of the technology alone will drive the desired outcomes.
Use a structured change approach that explicitly addresses behaviour change barriers — such as skill gaps, role uncertainty, and resistance to new workflows — alongside technical implementation.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - nature.com
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear due to limited snippet information. The theoretical framework (cognitive appraisal of stress and Job Demands-Resources model) is internationally applicable, but geographic scope, sample characteristics, and sector representation cannot be determined from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger job crafting through two distinct pathways: one via stress appraisal (threat vs. challenge) and another via resource-demand evaluation. Understanding which pathway your employees use helps tailor interventions—some may need reassurance about AI threats, while others need guidance on leveraging AI as a work resource.

Frame AI introduction to employees as an opportunity to redesign their work (job crafting) rather than purely as a threat. This dual-pathway insight suggests that how you position AI (as a challenge to master vs. a threat to manage) will influence whether employees proactively shape their roles positively.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without disclosed empirical research, methodology, or specific geographic scope. Findings likely reflect US higher education and business school viewpoint.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and workflows in your organisation where AI adoption is most feasible, then pilot behaviour-change interventions (e.g. training, coaching, feedback loops) tailored to those use cases rather than organisation-wide rollout.

Address potential resistance to AI adoption by engaging employees early in shaping how AI tools are implemented and used in their roles — this co-design approach increases buy-in and reduces defensive behaviour.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and regions, but lacks transparent methodology and may reflect biases toward large organisations with significant AI budgets.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI transformation across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to identify which stage you're currently in and what behavioural or structural shifts are needed to progress.
Focus change efforts on the gap between pilot projects and sustained organisational impact — most failures occur when moving from initial AI adoption to widespread, business-critical use.

Align incentive structures and role clarity across teams at each horizon; adoption requires technical enablers, scaling requires operational integration, and impact requires cultural buy-in and accountability measures.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet. The approach-avoidance framework is theoretically applicable across contexts, but findings may be limited by sector, geography, or organisational type.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption communications around approach motivations (new opportunities, skill development) rather than avoidance fears (job loss, displacement) to encourage constructive job crafting rather than withdrawal.

Monitor for bimodal employee responses to AI adoption — some will proactively reshape their roles while others may retreat; tailor support interventions to each response pattern to maintain engagement and productivity.

Use job crafting as an indicator of psychological safety during AI transitions — employees who feel secure enough to actively reshape their work suggest the organisational change is being managed effectively.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG insights are based on consulting engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect clients who can afford major consulting projects, potentially skewing toward larger, better-resourced organisations.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability issue, not just a technology implementation — success depends on identifying which roles need upskilling, retraining, or restructuring before deploying AI tools.
Design change management that addresses employee concerns about job displacement directly rather than assuming adoption will follow from technology availability alone.

Map your current workforce capabilities against future AI-enabled roles early in transformation planning, so you can plan targeted learning interventions and career pathways rather than reacting to capability gaps post-implementation.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — this appears to be a news summary of a single study; full methodological details, sample size, and geographic scope are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, competitiveness) may paradoxically attract romantic partners in the short term, despite being associated with relationship instability — a counterintuitive clash between initial appeal and long-term compatibility.

The finding challenges the assumption that toxic personality traits universally repel potential partners; some narcissistic traits can trigger attraction signals, raising questions about what draws us to people who may not treat us well.

This highlights a deeper puzzle in human mating psychology: why we're sometimes attracted to traits (arrogance, dominance, antagonism) that evolutionary logic and relationship research suggest should be red flags.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in snippet. Likely limited to lab-based memory tasks; real-world applicability to naturally occurring surprises unclear.
takeaways: Your personality shape how well you remember shocking moments — some people's brains are naturally wired to lock in surprising events better than others.
The finding hints at why eyewitness accounts vary so much: it's not just about what happened, but who's doing the remembering and how their personality filters unexpected information.
Counterintuitive insight: being surprised doesn't automatically make a memory stick — your personality traits matter as much as the surprise itself in determining what you'll actually recall later.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven summary of neuroimaging research; original study details not provided, so cannot assess sample size, methodology rigour, or whether findings replicate across populations.
takeaways: Brain imaging has detected structural or functional differences in people diagnosed with psychopathy — a counterintuitive finding that challenges assumptions that psychopathic traits are purely behavioural or learned.

The 'shocking' framing suggests the biological basis of psychopathy may be more concrete than previously thought, raising interesting questions about where personality traits live in the brain and whether they're hardwired or changeable.
This touches on a fascinating paradox: if psychopathy has a neural signature, does that make it more or less 'real' as a diagnosis, and does it change how we think about moral responsibility?

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — methodology and sample details not provided. Likely limited to English-language wine reviews from specific platforms, which may not represent all wine drinkers or cultures.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from seemingly mundane consumer writing like wine reviews — the language people use to describe taste reveals something about who they are.
Wine reviews are a surprisingly rich window into personality: the words people choose (descriptive detail, emotional language, technical jargon) correlate with measurable personality differences.

This hints at a broader insight: our everyday writing and product opinions leave personality fingerprints that machines can now read — intriguing for anyone curious about what our casual language reveals about us.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin study methodology and sample characteristics, which are not detailed in the snippet. Twin studies typically assume equal environments for monozygotic and dizygotic twins, which may not fully hold in practice.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs appear to have a significant genetic component — surprising because we often assume political views are purely learned or ideologically chosen.
Twin studies reveal that nature and nurture interact in shaping authoritarianism, challenging the common assumption that politics is entirely about upbringing or rational conviction.

This finding is counterintuitive because it suggests some people may be temperamentally predisposed toward authoritarian thinking, which could reshape how we understand political polarisation and persuasion.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI validity, but findings are constrained by the quality and consistency of underlying studies on leadership prediction.
takeaways: Despite its popularity in corporate training and team-building, MBTI has weak empirical support for predicting actual leadership behaviors — a surprising disconnect between what many organisations believe and what research shows.

The headline finding: MBTI types don't reliably forecast who will be an effective leader, making those expensive off-site workshops sorting people into personality boxes potentially more fun than functionally useful.

This matters because millions of professionals worldwide get sorted into four-letter boxes annually, yet the evidence suggests personality type alone is a poor leadership crystal ball — revealing the gap between intuitive appeal and scientific validity in popular business tools.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size (not detailed in snippet). The relationship between inclusive leadership, psychological safety, and innovation may vary across cultural contexts and organisational types; leader power distance orientation effects may differ in low vs. high power-distance cultures.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership that reduces perceived power distance strengthens the link between psychological safety and team innovation — consider actively signalling approachability and inviting input from all levels to unlock innovation potential.

Psychological safety alone may not drive innovation; pair it with genuinely inclusive leadership behaviours (e.g., soliciting dissenting views, acknowledging mistakes, distributing decision-making) to create conditions where teams feel safe to take creative risks.

Be aware that leader power distance orientation — whether leaders maintain or flatten hierarchy — moderates how psychological safety translates into innovative outcomes; reflect on your own leadership stance and its impact on team dynamics.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across geographies and sectors, though representativeness depends on PwC's sampling methodology and weighting; may overrepresent responses from larger organisations and developed markets.
takeaways: Identify the top workforce anxieties (likely around job security, AI, economic uncertainty) from this 2025 snapshot to benchmark psychological safety interventions against current employee concerns in your organisation.

Use survey findings on hope vs. fear ratios by region or sector to tailor safety messaging — organisations where fear outweighs hope may need stronger leadership communication and transparent policies to rebuild trust.

Cross-reference global trends with your local workforce data to pinpoint gaps: if your Australian employees report lower psychological safety than global peers on specific issues, design targeted interventions to address those vulnerabilities.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - nature.com
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity from title and snippet alone; full methodology and sample characteristics would determine whether findings generalise across geographies and sectors. Geographic scope and sample size cannot be confirmed from the provided information.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent investment in psychological safety and ethical leadership practices may increase employee depression and mental health risks — organisations should pair technical implementation with clear ethical frameworks and leadership training.

Psychological safety acts as a critical mediator between AI adoption and employee wellbeing; leaders should actively foster a culture where employees feel safe raising concerns about AI systems, job security, and ethical issues without fear of retaliation.

Ethical leadership is essential during AI transitions — leaders must visibly model ethical decision-making around AI use, be transparent about its impact on roles and workflows, and demonstrate commitment to employee welfare alongside business outcomes.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on multi-country client data and consulting experience, but specific sample composition, size, and methodology are not transparent from the snippet alone. Findings likely generalisable to large, multinational organisations but may not reflect SMEs or non-Western contexts.
takeaways: Create explicit norms where employees from underrepresented groups feel safe speaking up without fear of social or professional consequences — this reduces hidden hierarchies that prevent diverse perspectives from surfacing.

Use psychological safety interventions to close performance gaps: employees who feel psychologically safe are more likely to ask for help, admit mistakes, and contribute ideas, which levels access to development opportunities across demographic groups.
Measure psychological safety alongside diversity metrics — it is a mechanism that makes inclusion programmes actually work, not a standalone nice-to-have.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a brief Deloitte overview without detailed methodology, sample description, or geographic scope provided in the snippet. Findings likely reflect Deloitte's consulting experience but generalisability to other sectors and regions is unclear.
takeaways: Prioritise developing human capabilities (communication, collaboration, trust-building) alongside technical skills to improve team performance, as these create the foundation for psychological safety.
Audit your team's current capability mix — identify gaps in interpersonal and emotional intelligence, not just task competence, to target development efforts where they matter most for team cohesion.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely synthesises international research but specific geographic scope and organisational contexts not evident from title and snippet alone. Findings on co-skilling and job insecurity may vary across labour markets and regulatory environments.
takeaways: Implement formal co-skilling programmes that pair AI upskilling with reassurance about role security to reduce psychological threat and build trust in AI transitions.
Combine skills development with visible organisational support (transparent communication, career pathways, mentoring) to mitigate job insecurity and foster psychological safety during AI adoption.
Frame AI as a tool that augments rather than replaces roles; this framing combined with genuine upskilling investment is more effective at reducing anxiety than skills training alone.
